key_terms.meaning: Electrical input → light source (LED or laser) → fiber → photodetector → electrical output
Carrier is a light wave of frequency about 2×10¹⁴ Hz, so huge modulation bandwidth is available
Silica fiber loss can be below 0.5 dB/km at 1300–1550 nm, so repeaters sit tens of km apart
No metallic path between transmitter and receiver, so no ground loops, no spark hazard, no lightning pick-up
At a boundary to a rarer medium, light with θ₁ > θc is fully reflected back, no refracted ray
θc = sin⁻¹(n₂/n₁), the smallest incidence angle at the core–cladding boundary that gives TIR
θa = sin⁻¹(NA), the largest half-angle of an input cone whose rays are guided
NA = √(n₁² − n₂²) = n₀ sin θa; measures the light-gathering power of the fiber
A ray that misses the fiber axis and travels as a helix; it needs a stricter bound condition than NA alone
One discrete field pattern that travels down the guide without changing its shape
A slab of higher index n₁ between two lower-index layers n₂; light is confined in one direction only
Core index n₁ is uniform and drops sharply to n₂ at the cladding boundary
Core index falls smoothly from the axis outward, so rays curve and arrive together, reducing modal dispersion
Core so small that only the LP₀₁ mode is guided; no modal dispersion
λc = 2πa·NA / 2.405; the fiber is single-mode only for λ > λc
V = (2πa/λ)·NA, the normalized frequency that sets how many modes a fiber guides
v_p = ω/β = c/n, the speed at which one crest of the wave advances
v_g = dω/dβ, the speed of the pulse envelope; signal delay follows v_g, not v_p
A high-index strip of finite width on a chip; confines light in two directions
A range of wavelengths that cannot propagate through a periodic dielectric structure in some direction

takeaways: A fiber link is just a light source, a glass guide and a detector, but the glass guide removes the bandwidth limit of copper.
Light stays in the core because of total internal reflection, and the acceptance angle tells you how well you can launch into it.
Numerical aperture is the single number that links the refractive indices to the launch cone.
Maxwell's equations in a layered dielectric allow only discrete field patterns, which we call modes.
Step-index fiber is simple; graded-index fiber trades a harder profile for much less modal dispersion.
Whether a fiber is single-mode depends on the wavelength you use, not on the fiber alone.
The speed of your data is set by group velocity; phase velocity is not what the bits follow.
On a chip, the same reflection idea is squeezed into a strip a few hundred nanometres wide.
Periodic dielectrics can forbid light in a band of wavelengths and so guide or trap it.
Numbers matter in this unit: NA, V, λc and delay are all short calculations an examiner will ask for.
bank_note: Long answers are expected to carry a clean derivation of acceptance angle and numerical aperture, the mode count from V and cutoff wavelength, a three-way comparison of fiber types, and short numerical substitutions with units at every step.

bank.q: Draw the block diagram of a general optical fiber communication system and explain the function of each block. List four advantages of optical fiber over copper cable, with one reason for each.
outline: Blocks: information source, electrical transmitter, drive circuit, light source (LED/laser), fiber cable, photodetector (PIN/APD), amplifier, signal processing, output
Light source converts current to optical power; fiber carries it; detector converts optical power back to current
Advantages: wide bandwidth (light carrier ~10¹⁴ Hz), low loss (<0.5 dB/km), electrical isolation (dielectric), small size and weight, security (no easy tapping, no radiation)
One line each on why the advantage exists

bank.q: State the laws of reflection and refraction. Define the critical angle and derive its expression. Explain total internal reflection and the two conditions needed for it.
outline: Snell's law n₁ sin θ₁ = n₂ sin θ₂ with terms defined
θc when θ₂ = 90°, giving θc = sin⁻¹(n₂/n₁)
Conditions: n₁ > n₂ and θ₁ > θc
Result: all energy reflected, evanescent field in cladding beyond the boundary
Ray diagram with angles marked from the normal

bank.q: Define numerical aperture of a step-index fiber and derive NA = √(n₁² − n₂²). Relate it to the acceptance angle.
outline: Definition: NA = n₀ sin θa
Meridional ray meets the boundary at angle (90° − θa) inside the core
Apply Snell's law at the launch face and then the TIR condition at the boundary
Squaring and adding gives sin θa = √(n₁² − n₂²)/n₀
For air n₀ = 1, so NA = √(n₁² − n₂²) ≈ n₁√(2Δ) with Δ = (n₁ − n₂)/n₁
State units: NA is dimensionless

bank.q: Explain electromagnetic mode theory for a planar dielectric guide. Why does the guide support only discrete field patterns? Define mode number and the meaning of the mode field picture.
outline: Start from Maxwell's equations, write the wave equation in each layer
Field must be a standing pattern in the core and decaying (evanescent) in the cladding
Boundary conditions: tangential E and H continuous at both interfaces
These give a transcendental eigenvalue equation whose solutions are discrete β values
Each β gives a mode: a fixed transverse pattern that propagates unchanged
Mode number m = number of field nulls in the core; higher m sits closer to cutoff

bank.q: A step-index fiber has core index 1.50 and cladding index 1.48. Calculate the numerical aperture, the acceptance angle in air, and the critical angle at the core–cladding boundary.
outline: Comment: NA is dimensionless; angles measured from the axis for θa and from the normal for θc

bank.q: A multimode step-index fiber has core radius 25 μm, NA = 0.22, and is used at λ = 1300 nm. Find the V number and the number of guided modes. Is the fiber single-mode? Repeat for λ = 850 nm.
outline: V = 2πa·NA/λ with a in metres and λ in metres
Modes M ≈ V²/2 ≈ 354 (meridional estimate); mention the more accurate M ≈ V²/4 for step index if the syllabus uses it
At 850 nm: V ≈ 40.7, so many more modes
V > 2.405 in both cases, so not single mode at either wavelength

bank.q: Explain how a graded-index profile reduces intermodal dispersion. A graded-index fiber has n₁ = 1.48 at the axis, n₂ = 1.46 at the cladding and profile parameter α = 2. Compare its modal delay spread qualitatively with a step-index fiber of the same NA.
outline: Index falls as n(r) = n₁√(1 − 2Δ(r/a)^α) for r < a
Rays away from the axis travel in a lower-index region, so they move faster
Off-axis ray path is longer but average speed is higher; the two effects cancel to first order
Optimum α is about 2 for minimum dispersion
Delay spread falls roughly by a factor of Δ (about 100×) compared with step index
Consequence: graded-index multimode gives much higher bandwidth at the same core size

bank.q: A 10 km link uses fiber with group index 1.47. Find the group velocity and the pulse delay. Distinguish clearly between phase velocity and group velocity.
outline: Delay = L/v_g = 10⁴/2.04×10⁸ ≈ 49 μs
Phase velocity v_p = ω/β = c/n: speed of a single crest, can exceed c/n_g in some cases
Group velocity v_g = dω/dβ: speed of the envelope, carries information
Timing, dispersion and bit-rate limits all use v_g

bank.q: A fiber has cutoff wavelength 1.20 μm. Explain what happens if the same fiber is used at 850 nm and at 1550 nm. Support your answer with the V number and the meaning of 2.405.
outline: λc = 2πa·NA/2.405; below λc the V number exceeds 2.405
At 850 nm, V = 2.405 × (1200/850) ≈ 3.4 > 2.405: several modes travel, modal dispersion appears
At 1550 nm, V = 2.405 × (1200/1550) ≈ 1.86 < 2.405: single-mode operation
Only LP₀₁ travels; LP₁₁ is cut off
Practical note: bending loss rises as V falls too far below 1

bank.q: Compare step-index multimode, graded-index multimode and single-mode fibers on core size, NA, dispersion, bandwidth and cost of connectors. Recommend one type for a campus LAN and one for a 1000 km trunk, giving reasons.
outline: Table: core 50–100 μm / 50–62.5 μm / 8–10 μm; NA about 0.3 / 0.2 / 0.1
Dispersion: high modal / reduced modal / no modal, material only
Bandwidth-length product increases across the three
LED can launch into multimode, cheap connectors, easy splicing; single mode needs laser and tight alignment
Campus LAN: multimode graded index, short distance, cheap connectors
Trunk: single mode at 1550 nm, lowest loss and dispersion, fewest repeaters
Mention cost per km versus cost per connector

bank.q: Explain modal dispersion and material dispersion. Show how core profile and operating wavelength affect each, and argue why single-mode operation is preferred for long-haul links.
outline: Modal dispersion: different modes have different group velocities, pulse broadens as modes separate
Material dispersion: n depends on λ, so a source with finite spectral width spreads the pulse; zero around 1300 nm in silica
Waveguide dispersion adds to material dispersion
Graded index reduces modal dispersion by equalising path and speed
Single mode removes modal dispersion completely, leaving only chromatic dispersion, which is small at 1550 nm and can be managed
Bit rate limit from broadening: Δt must be a small fraction of the bit period

bank.q: Describe photonic crystals and the photonic band gap. Contrast index guiding with band-gap guiding, and explain how a photonic crystal fiber and a photonic crystal waveguide use these ideas.
outline: Periodic arrangement of dielectrics with period comparable to λ; Bragg scattering in all directions
Band gap: wavelengths that cannot propagate; arises from symmetry and periodicity, not from absorption
Defect in the lattice creates a localised mode inside the gap → cavity or waveguide
Index guiding: light held by TIR in a high-index core (solid-core PCF)
Band-gap guiding: light held in a low-index or hollow core by the surrounding periodic cladding
Line defect in a 2D slab gives a sharp-bend waveguide on a chip
Uses: low-loss hollow-core fiber, microcavities, filters, slow light

bank.q: Explain strip and channel waveguides used in integrated optics. Why is light confined in two dimensions, and what practical difficulties appear when the guide is made very small?
outline: High-index film on a lower-index substrate plus a lower-index cover; etching leaves a strip of width w
Vertical confinement by the index step, horizontal confinement by the side walls or a rib profile
Solve the slab problem in each direction; the effective-index method reduces it to a planar problem
Single-mode condition depends on w, thickness and index step
Difficulties: scattering loss from sidewall roughness, coupling loss to fiber because of mode-size mismatch, polarization dependence
Uses: splitters, modulators, ring resonators, chip-to-chip optical links

bank.q: Skew rays carry a large share of the power in a multimode fiber. Explain how a skew ray differs from a meridional ray, why the simple NA formula does not bound it, and what practical effects follow.
outline: Meridional ray passes through the axis; its path stays in one plane
Skew ray misses the axis and travels as a helix, with an azimuthal component of the wave vector
Bound condition needs both the axial and the azimuthal component to satisfy TIR, giving a stricter limit than NA
Skew rays have longer paths, so they arrive later and add to modal dispersion
They can be launched by an off-axis source and are hard to strip out
Practical effect: measured NA with a large-area launch can differ from the theoretical value

glossary.def: The central high-index region of a fiber that carries the light.
The lower-index layer around the core that makes total internal reflection possible.
The protective plastic coating outside the cladding; it carries no light.
A fiber whose core index is uniform and changes abruptly at the cladding.
A fiber whose core index decreases smoothly from the axis to the cladding.
n = c/v, the ratio of light speed in vacuum to that in the medium.
Δ = (n₁ − n₂)/n₁, typically 0.01 for multimode and 0.003 for single-mode fiber.
A ray whose path crosses the fiber axis and lies in one plane.
A ray that never crosses the axis and follows a helical path.
The cone of input rays, of half-angle θa, that the fiber can guide.
The sine of the acceptance angle in air; a measure of light-gathering power.
A discrete, self-consistent field distribution that propagates without changing shape.
Linearly polarised mode; the weakly guiding approximation used to label fiber modes such as LP₀₁.
V = 2πa·NA/λ, the normalized frequency that sets the mode count.
The wavelength below which a fiber stops being single-mode.
A fiber that guides only the LP₀₁ mode at the working wavelength.
A fiber that guides many modes, with a core of roughly 50–100 μm.
Pulse broadening caused by different modes travelling at different group velocities.
The speed of a single crest of the wave, v_p = ω/β.
The speed of the pulse envelope, v_g = dω/dβ.
A slab of high-index material that confines light in one transverse direction.
A raised strip or rib of high index that confines light in two transverse directions.
A dielectric structure whose refractive index varies periodically with a period near the wavelength of light.
A band of wavelengths that cannot propagate through a photonic crystal in a given direction.
A fiber whose cladding contains a regular array of air holes, guiding by index contrast or by band gap.
β/k₀, the equivalent index seen by a mode; used to reduce 2D problems to 1D.
